meta.blurb: Nora Bell has come to Willow Bay to sign some papers and leave. Instead she finds five leaking boats, a note from her late aunt asking her to stay one summer, and a quiet boat builder next door.
meta.bible: Nora Bell: a city office worker in her late twenties, proud, prickly and slow to ask for help; Dot's niece. Dot: Nora's Aunt, who died this spring and left her the boat hut; funny, stubborn, winner of the Willow Cup many times. Eli Okafor: a boat builder who rents the workshop next door; quiet, kind and steady; his father taught him to build boats and has died. Biscuit: Eli's big brown dog who steals sandwiches. Mrs Pruitt: runs the tea shop, Dot's friend for fifty years, loves gossip. Sam: a shy boy who learns to row. Mr Grant: from Harbour Group, a company that wants to buy the land and build a hotel and marina. Willow Bay: a small seaside town with a jetty, a quay and a tea shop. Gull Island: a small green island about a mile across the bay with an old stone shelter. The Willow Cup: a rowing race for pairs on the last Saturday of August. Dot: the name Eli paints on his racing boat. Bell and Okafor Boats: the new sign. September: the deadline is the first of September. Voice and tone: warm, light, funny and romantic, a gentle slow-burn summer love story with a happy ending.

B1B2: Nora stepped off the bus in the pouring rain, holding a single suitcase. She had not been to Willow Bay since she was a child, and the town looked smaller than she remembered.
Her Aunt Dot had left her the boat hut at the end of the jetty, and the key still turned easily. Inside, five rowing boats sat in the dust, and every one of them needed paint.
Pinned above the workbench was a note in Dot's careful handwriting. It said, “Stay one summer before you sell, my dear, and then do as you like.”
Next door, a tall man with paint on his hands was working on a half-built wooden boat. He glanced at Nora, nodded once, and went back to his work without a word.
Nora sat down on the jetty to eat, and a large brown dog appeared from nowhere. Before she could say a word, it had taken her whole sandwich and run away.
Mrs Pruitt ran the tea shop on the corner, and she had known Nora's aunt for fifty years. Everyone who came in that afternoon wanted to tell Nora how much they had loved Dot.
That evening a man named Mr Grant telephoned from Harbour Group, a company that builds hotels. He wanted to buy the land by the first of September and offered a very good price.
Nora pushed one of the boats into the shallow water to test it. Within a minute, water was bubbling up through the planks and rising around her ankles.
The man from next door, whose name was Eli, offered to mend the boats for nothing. Nora thanked him stiffly and said that she could manage by herself.
All the next morning Nora tried to patch the leaks with tar and tape. By lunchtime she was covered in black from head to foot, and the boat was no better.
In the afternoon Nora walked next door and admitted that she needed help. Eli only smiled, picked up his tools, and said that he had been waiting for her to ask.
By Saturday, two boats were ready, and a family of four arrived to hire one. Nora took their money, pushed them off, and watched with her heart in her mouth.
Nora could not row a straight line, and she hated being bad at things. So Eli met her at dawn every day that week and showed her how to hold the oars.
One morning the bay was perfectly still, and the rising sun turned the water to gold. Nora stopped rowing and, for the first time in months, felt completely happy.
Mrs Pruitt told Nora about the Willow Cup, a race for pairs of rowers held on the last Saturday of August. Dot had won it many times, and the photograph on the wall showed her holding the silver cup.
Back in the hut, Nora opened a cupboard and found a row of tarnished trophies. Beside them lay a thick notebook, in which Dot had written about every race and every summer.
Eli took Nora into his workshop to see the long wooden boat for two that he was building. His father had taught him to build boats, he said, and this one was meant for the Willow Cup.
On a hot evening, Nora and Eli swam out from the jetty while the sky turned pink. They floated on their backs, talking about nothing, until the first stars came out.
The summer fair filled the harbour with music, lights and the smell of fried onions. Eli, who claimed he never danced, was pulled into a circle by Mrs Pruitt and found himself holding Nora's hand.
That night Nora lay awake in the little room above the hut and thought about Eli's hand. It was only a dance, she told herself, and she was only here for the summer.
Mr Grant arrived in a shiny car, wearing a suit that was far too warm for the weather. He spread his plans on Nora's workbench and showed her where the hotel and the marina would stand.
After Mr Grant left, Nora studied the plans more carefully and went cold. Eli rented his workshop from her family, so the sale would put him out of his home.
Nora folded the plans small and pushed them to the back of a drawer. She told herself she would tell Eli when she had decided what to do, and not before.
Nora threw herself into work to stop thinking, and painted the boats in bright colours. People began to stop on the jetty to take photographs, and bookings grew every day.
A shy boy called Sam started coming to the hut for rowing lessons. He hardly spoke at first, but Nora understood him, because she had been shy at his age too.
At the end of the week Sam rowed all the way across the cove by himself. Nora and Eli cheered from the jetty, and Sam's face lit up like a lamp.
On Sunday, Eli suggested a picnic on Gull Island, a small green island across the bay. They rowed over together with a basket, a blanket and Biscuit sitting proudly in the front.
Late in the afternoon, a thick white fog rolled in from the sea. Within minutes they could not see the mainland, and Eli said that it would be foolish to row back in the dark.
There was an old stone hut on the island, and Eli lit a small fire inside it. He telephoned Mrs Pruitt so that nobody would worry, and then they sat down to wait.

Sitting by the fire, they talked for hours about everything they had never told anyone. Nora admitted that she had always left places before she could miss them, and Eli said that he had never left Willow Bay at all.
At dawn the fog thinned and turned pink, and they stood together at the water's edge. Eli leaned closer, but a loud ferry horn sounded across the bay, and they stepped apart, laughing.
They rowed home through the last wisps of fog and found Mrs Pruitt waiting on the jetty with a flask of tea. She looked at their faces, said nothing, and smiled to herself all day.
That evening they sat at the end of the jetty with their feet in the water. This time there was no ferry horn, and Eli kissed her, softly, as the sun went down.
News travels fast in a small town, and by lunchtime everyone knew. People smiled at them in the street, and Mrs Pruitt put an extra cherry on top of their cake.
In the middle of this happiness, Nora's phone rang, and it was her boss in the city. He told her that the job she had always wanted was hers, but she must start on the first of September.
Then Mr Grant telephoned again, and this time his price was much higher. He said that the offer would end on the first of September, and Nora felt the days closing in.
One afternoon Eli went to the drawer to borrow a pencil and found the folded plans. He read them slowly, and his face changed as he understood what he was seeing.
Eli asked how long she had known, and Nora could only say, “Since July.” He told her that she had let him fall in love with her while she planned to knock down his home.
Eli walked back to his workshop with Biscuit, and he did not look back. For three days the big doors stayed closed, and no hammering came from next door.
Nora went to the tea shop and told Mrs Pruitt everything. The old woman listened without interrupting, and then she said that Dot had once refused an offer for the hut too.
That night Nora opened Dot's notebook at the last page and read it by lamplight. It was a letter, written only a few weeks before Dot died, and it was addressed to her.
Dot wrote that she had never asked anyone for help, and it had made her life lonelier than it needed to be. She hoped that Nora would be braver, and would let the people of Willow Bay in.
At dawn Nora telephoned Mr Grant and told him that the hut was not for sale. He argued politely for ten minutes, and she thanked him and ended the call.
Then she wrote to her boss in the city and thanked him for the job. She said that she would not be coming back, and pressed the button with a shaking finger.
That evening Nora stood up in the tea shop and told the whole town that she was staying. Everybody cheered, and Mrs Pruitt cried into her apron.
Nora wrote a note and pinned it to Eli's workshop door. It said that she was sorry, that she was staying, and that she needed a partner for the Willow Cup.
On the morning of the race, the workshop doors swung open at last. Eli pushed his finished boat down to the jetty, and on its side he had painted the name Dot.
Ten boats lined up at the start across the bay, and half of Willow Bay watched from the shore. Nora's hands shook on the oars, but Eli, sitting behind her, said that she was ready.
For most of the race they stayed in the middle of the fleet. In the final stretch they began to row as one, and they crossed the line first by no more than a hand's length.
After the race Eli told Nora that he had read her note a hundred times. In autumn a new sign went up over the hut, and it read Bell and Okafor Boats.
C1C2: It was raining hard when Nora Bell stepped off the last bus of the day, dragging a suitcase that seemed heavier with every puddle. Willow Bay lay below her, a huddle of grey roofs and bobbing masts that she had not seen since she was twelve years old. She had come, she told herself firmly, only to sign some papers and leave again.

Aunt Dot's boat hut stood at the very end of the jetty, its blue paint peeling and its door swollen with years of sea air. Inside, five rowing boats lay upside down in the gloom like sleeping animals, and the whole place smelled of salt, tar and old rope. Nora ran a finger along a hull and left a clean line in the dust.

Pinned above the workbench was a note in Dot's neat, upright handwriting, and it was clearly meant for Nora alone. “Stay one summer before you sell,” it said, “and if you still want to go in September, I will not mind a bit.” Nora laughed out loud, because her aunt had always known how to win an argument from beyond the grave.

In the workshop next door, a tall man with sawdust in his hair was bent over the ribs of a half-built wooden boat, humming tunelessly to himself. When he noticed Nora watching, he gave her a single polite nod, as one might greet a stranger on a train, and returned to his planing. She decided at once that he was rude, although she could not have said exactly why.

She had barely unwrapped her lunch on the jetty when a large, shaggy dog came bounding along the boards, studied her with great seriousness, and snatched the sandwich out of her hand. By the time she had finished shouting, the thief was already trotting back toward the workshop, wagging his tail. A deep voice called out that the dog's name was Biscuit and that he was very sorry, though he did not sound it.

At the tea shop on the corner, Mrs Pruitt wrapped Nora in a hug, set a slice of lemon cake before her, and refused all talk of payment. One by one the customers drifted over to say what Dot had meant to them, and by the end of the hour Nora's eyes were stinging. She had known her aunt as a writer of postcards, but this town had known her as a friend.

That evening Mr Grant of Harbour Group telephoned from his office in the city, speaking in the warm voice of someone who has made many such calls. His company wished to build a hotel beside the bay, he explained, and the land under Dot's hut was exactly what they needed. He named a price so generous that Nora had to sit down on an upturned bucket.

Determined to see what she had inherited, Nora dragged the lightest boat down the slipway and climbed in with wobbling confidence. Within a minute, water was welling up through every seam, and the little vessel settled gently beneath her like a tired cow lowering itself onto the grass. She stood knee-deep in the bay, holding an oar, and wondered what on earth she was doing.

The tall neighbour, who introduced himself as Eli Okafor, waded out without being asked and offered to mend all five boats for nothing. Nora, who disliked owing anything to anyone, thanked him in her coolest voice and said that she would manage by herself. Eli shrugged, whistled for his dog, and said that the offer would not go away.

All the next morning she wrestled with tar, tape and a book of instructions she did not understand, and by lunchtime she was black from her elbows to her ankles. The boat looked worse than before, and Biscuit, who had come to supervise, sat watching her with an expression of deep pity. From next door came the unmistakable sound of someone trying very hard not to laugh.

When the sun had dropped low, Nora swallowed her pride, walked next door, and admitted that she had no idea what she was doing. Eli put down his plane without a trace of triumph, collected his tools, and said that a boat always takes two pairs of hands, even if only one of them knows what it is doing. Together they knelt in the gloom of the hut and began to mend the first hull.

By Saturday two of the boats had been mended and painted, and a family of four wandered down the jetty to ask whether they could hire one. Nora, who had never taken money for anything but a day's work at a desk, handed over the oars with trembling hands and pushed them gently away from the steps. They wobbled, they spun in a circle, and they came back an hour later sunburned and delighted.

Nora could not row in a straight line, and the humiliation of watching her customers do better than she did became more than she could bear. Eli, who seemed to understand this without being told, began to meet her at dawn on the jetty each morning, correcting her grip with a gentleness that surprised them both. By the fourth day she had stopped going in circles, and by the end of the week she could keep the bow pointed at the far headland.

One morning the bay lay perfectly still, and the rising sun poured itself across the water until every ripple seemed to be made of gold. Nora let the oars drift and sat with her face turned to the light, aware that something tight inside her, which she had carried for years, had quietly come undone. She realised that she could not remember the last time she had felt so entirely unhurried.

Mrs Pruitt led Nora to a faded photograph on the tea shop wall and explained that it showed the Willow Cup, the bay's rowing race for pairs, held every year on the last Saturday of August. Dot had entered it for forty summers, she said proudly, and had won it more times than anyone could count. In the picture her aunt stood grinning in wet boots, holding a silver cup above her head like a flag.

Back in the hut, Nora opened a stiff cupboard and found a row of tarnished trophies, each with a year engraved beneath it. Beside them lay a thick notebook, its cover stained with tea, in which Dot had recorded every race, every storm and every customer for decades. Nora turned a few pages, then closed it carefully, feeling that she had been invited somewhere but was not yet ready to go in.

Eli led her into his workshop, where a slender wooden racing boat rested on its stand, as graceful as a sleeping swan. His father, he said quietly, had been a boat builder too, and had taught him everything before he died, and this was the first boat Eli had made without him. It was meant for the Willow Cup, though he had never found a partner he trusted to row it.

On a breathless evening after the hottest day of the summer, Nora and Eli swam out from the jetty while the sky faded from pink to violet. They floated on their backs and talked about nothing in particular, and the hours slipped away so quietly that neither of them noticed the first stars coming out. Nora climbed the ladder afterward with the odd feeling that she had forgotten to be on her guard.

The summer fair filled the harbour with fiddle music, paper lanterns and the smell of sugar, and the whole town seemed to have come out to dance on the quay. Eli, who had announced that he never danced, was seized by Mrs Pruitt and delivered into the middle of a circle, where he found himself holding Nora's hand. Neither of them let go until the music stopped, and neither mentioned it afterward.

That night Nora lay awake in the little room above the boat hut, listening to the water slap against the posts and thinking about the warmth of Eli's hand. It had been nothing, she told herself, a moment of music and lantern light, and she was only here until September. But the argument sounded thin even to her, and the sea did not appear to believe it either.

Mr Grant arrived in a gleaming car, wearing a suit far too warm for the weather, and unrolled a set of glossy plans across Nora's workbench. They showed a vast white hotel with a glass front and a marina for yachts, standing exactly where the boat hut and the jetty stood now. He smiled as he spoke, and Nora noticed that he never once looked at the bay.

When Mr Grant had gone, Nora bent over the plans again and felt her stomach drop. Eli's workshop appeared nowhere on them, for the simple reason that the company meant to knock it down, and since he rented it from Dot's family, the choice to sell would now be hers alone. Eli, she realised with a slow, sinking horror, had not the faintest idea that any of this was coming.

Nora folded the plans into a small square and pushed them to the very back of a drawer, as if hiding them might make them less real. She would tell Eli, she promised herself, as soon as she had decided what to do, because it seemed unkind to hurt him with a problem she had not yet solved. It was a perfectly reasonable argument, she thought, and she did not believe a single word of it.

Nora threw herself into work to avoid thinking, painting the boats in cheerful shades of yellow, green and sky blue and hanging a hand-lettered sign over the door. Holidaymakers began to stop on the jetty to take photographs, and the little hut that had stood silent for a year filled with talk and sunburned laughter. By the end of the week she had turned away three families who had not booked.

A shy boy named Sam began to appear at the hut each afternoon, standing just outside the door until Nora invited him in for a rowing lesson. He hardly said a word at first, yet Nora understood him, for she remembered exactly how it felt to be small and quiet among confident people. She gave him the lightest oars in the hut, sat beside him on the steps, and told him there was no hurry at all.

At the end of the week Sam rowed the length of the cove entirely by himself, his tongue between his teeth and his eyes fixed on the horizon. Nora and Eli cheered from the jetty until they were hoarse, and when the boy stepped ashore his face was shining with the plain astonishment of having done something hard. Without a word, Eli put a hand on Nora's shoulder, and she found, to her own surprise, that she was happy to let it stay there.

On Sunday, Eli proposed a picnic on Gull Island, a small green hump of land about a mile across the bay. They rowed over together with a basket, a blanket and Biscuit sitting proudly in the bow like a figurehead, and spent the whole afternoon eating, talking and watching the gulls. It was the happiest day Nora could remember, and she was careful not to say so.

Late in the afternoon a thick white fog rolled in from the sea, swallowing the mainland, the boats and finally the beach itself. Eli, who had spent his whole life on this water, said calmly that rowing back blind would be foolish, and that they would be safer waiting until morning. Nora, who did not feel calm at all, said that this sounded like an excellent plan.

An old stone shelter stood among the rocks, left there long ago for stranded fishermen, and Eli soon had a small fire crackling in its corner. He telephoned Mrs Pruitt to say they were safe, which she received with suspicious calm, and then the two of them settled down to wait out the night. The fog pressed softly against the doorway, and the whole world seemed to have shrunk to the size of the firelight.

Wrapped in the same blanket, they talked for hours about everything they had never told anyone else. Nora admitted that she had always left places before she could miss them, and Eli confessed that he had never gone anywhere at all, for fear that the workshop would fall silent without him. Each of them listened as if the other were saying something wonderful and rare.

At dawn the fog thinned and turned pink, and the bay came slowly back into being, as though someone were painting it in. Eli leaned toward her at the water's edge, and Nora felt the whole world hold its breath, until the deep horn of the morning ferry boomed across the water and sent them apart, laughing helplessly. It was, Nora decided later, the most ridiculous and the most perfect interruption that had ever happened to anyone.

They rowed home through the last wisps of mist and found Mrs Pruitt waiting on the jetty with a flask of tea and an expression of enormous innocence. She asked no questions whatever, which told Nora precisely how many she was longing to ask, and she hummed a wedding march under her breath as she poured. Eli, scarlet to the ears, pretended to be extremely busy with the ropes and did not meet anyone's eye for a quarter of an hour.

That evening they sat at the end of the jetty with their feet dangling in the cool water, watching the sun slide behind the headland. This time there was no ferry, no dog and no interfering neighbour, and when Eli kissed her it felt like a question that she had been waiting all summer to answer. She answered it at some length, and the evening slowly turned from gold to violet without either of them noticing.

News travels at astonishing speed in a small town, and by lunchtime on Monday there was not a single person in Willow Bay who did not know. Neighbours smiled at them in the street, the baker gave them a free loaf, and Mrs Pruitt placed an extra cherry on top of their cake with the air of a woman who had won a bet. Nora, who had always hated being watched, found to her surprise that she did not mind it in the least.

In the middle of all this happiness, Nora's phone rang, and the voice of her old boss rolled out of it, brisk and bright. A promotion she had dreamed of for years, he said, was hers at last, but she would have to start on the first of September and could not delay it. She thanked him, put the phone down on the workbench, and stared at it as if it were a small hostile animal.

The very next morning Mr Grant telephoned again, and this time his offer was higher still, high enough to buy a small house in the city. It would end on the first of September, he reminded her pleasantly, and not a day after, and Nora felt the summer shrinking around her like a wet wool sweater. Two doors were opening, and both of them led away from where she stood.

One afternoon Eli opened the workbench drawer to borrow a pencil and found the folded plans lying at the back. He smoothed them out and read them slowly, and Nora, who had walked in with two mugs of tea, watched the colour leave his face as he understood what he was looking at. For a long moment the only sound in the hut was the water against the posts.

Eli asked how long she had known, and Nora, who had rehearsed a dozen explanations, could only say that it had been since July. He told her quietly that she had let him fall in love with her while she planned to flatten the place where his father had worked, and the quietness was far worse than shouting. She tried to say that she had meant to tell him, but the words sounded cheap even to her.

Eli whistled for Biscuit and walked back to his workshop without looking round, and the great doors closed behind him with a sound that echoed across the water. For three days no hammering came from next door, and the silence was so thorough that Nora began to find it hard to breathe. She had never before noticed how much she liked being accompanied by the noise of another person working.

Nora went to the tea shop and told Mrs Pruitt everything, from the first phone call to the folded plans in the drawer. The old woman listened without interrupting, stirred her tea thoughtfully, and then remarked that Dot too had once been offered a fortune for the hut and had sent the visitor away with a flea in his ear. Before Nora left, the old woman suggested quietly that she go home and read the last pages of Dot's notebook.

That night Nora sat on her narrow bed, opened Dot's notebook at the final page, and found that it was not a record of a race at all but a letter. It had been written only a few weeks before Dot died, in a hand that had grown a little shaky, and it began, “Dear Nora, I hope you came.” She read the rest slowly, then read it again, with one hand pressed over her mouth and the lamp burning low.

Dot wrote that she had never once asked anyone for help, and that her pride had made her life lonelier than it needed to be. The hut, she said, had never really been about boats, but about the people who came to it, and she hoped Nora would be braver than she had been. Nora read the last line three times, until the words blurred, and it said only, “Stay, if you can.”

At dawn Nora stood at the end of the jetty and telephoned Mr Grant to tell him that the hut, the jetty and the land beneath them were not for sale at any price. He argued politely for ten minutes, with growing impatience, and she thanked him, wished him luck elsewhere, and ended the call before her courage could change its mind. Above her, a line of gulls on the roof of the hut seemed to nod in grave and noisy approval.

Then she wrote to her boss in the city, thanking him warmly for the promotion and explaining that she would not be taking it. She read the message through twice, found that it held no regret whatsoever, and sent it before she could think of a single sensible reason to hesitate. For the first time in years, she felt as if she were running toward something instead of away.

That evening Nora stood on a chair in the tea shop and told the assembled town that she was not selling and that she intended to stay. The room erupted in cheering, somebody began to play the fiddle, and Mrs Pruitt wept happily into her apron while pressing a second slice of cake into Nora's hands. Only one person was missing from the celebration, and everyone in the room knew exactly who it was.

Nora wrote a note and pinned it to the door of Eli's silent workshop, taking more care over the handwriting than she had ever taken over anything. It said that she was truly sorry, that she was staying for good, and that she would very much like him to row the Willow Cup with her, if he could bear to. Then she walked back along the jetty in the early light, and for once she did not look behind her.

On the morning of the race, the great doors of the workshop swung open at last, and Eli walked out pushing his finished boat before him. It gleamed in the sunshine like a polished violin, and along its side, in small neat letters, he had painted the name Dot. He did not say a word, but only held out a pair of oars, and Nora took them.

Ten boats lined up across the mouth of the bay, and half of Willow Bay crowded the shore to watch, with Mrs Pruitt waving a tea towel at the front. Nora's hands shook on the oars, but Eli, sitting behind her, said in his low and steady voice that she had been ready since the first dawn on the water. The starter lifted his flag high above his head, and for a long moment the whole bay seemed to hold its breath.

For most of the race they stayed stubbornly in the middle of the fleet, until something shifted and the two of them began to move as a single creature, oars rising and falling like wings. In the final stretch they overtook three boats in a row and crossed the line first by no more than the width of a hand. From the quay came a roar so loud that Biscuit barked himself hoarse, and Nora felt, quite distinctly, that Dot was rowing with them.

After the prize-giving, Eli told Nora that he had read her note a hundred times and that he had no intention of ever being apart from her again. By the time the leaves turned, a new sign hung over the boat hut, painted by Sam in his best blue letters, and it read Bell and Okafor Boats. Nora looked at it from the jetty, with Eli's arm around her and Biscuit asleep on her feet, and understood that she was home.
